claim: Mice expressing truncated Disrupted-in-Schizophrenia 1 (Disc1) show depression-related behavior.
source: We find that mice expressing truncated Disrupted-in-Schizophrenia 1 (Disc1), which mirror a high-prevalence genotype for human psychiatric illness, show depression-related behavior.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by behavioral test data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Theta and low-gamma synchrony in the prelimbic cortex (PrlC) is impaired in Disc1 mice.
source: Theta and low-gamma synchrony in the prelimbic cortex (PrlC) is impaired in Disc1 mice and inversely correlated with the extent of behavioural despair.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract and supported by LFP recording data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Impaired theta and low-gamma synchrony is inversely correlated with the extent of behavioural despair in Disc1 mice.
source: Theta and low-gamma synchrony in the prelimbic cortex (PrlC) is impaired in Disc1 mice and inversely correlated with the extent of behavioural despair.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Weak theta activity in Disc1 mice is driven by the hippocampus.
source: While weak theta activity is driven by the hippocampus, disturbance of low-gamma oscillations is caused by local defects of parvalbumin (PV)-expressing fast-spiking interneurons (FS-INs).
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by cross-correlation analysis and hippocampal recordings shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Disturbance of low-gamma oscillations in Disc1 mice is caused by local defects of parvalbumin (PV)-expressing fast-spiking interneurons (FS-INs).
source: While weak theta activity is driven by the hippocampus, disturbance of low-gamma oscillations is caused by local defects of parvalbumin (PV)-expressing fast-spiking interneurons (FS-INs).
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by anatomical and electrophysiological data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The number of FS-INs is reduced in Disc1 mice.
source: The number of FS-INs is reduced, they receive fewer excitatory inputs, and form fewer release sites on targets.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by immunohistochemical quantification shown in Figure 3A.

claim: FS-INs in Disc1 mice receive fewer excitatory inputs.
source: The number of FS-INs is reduced, they receive fewer excitatory inputs, and form fewer release sites on targets.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by spEPSC recordings shown in Figure 4E.

claim: FS-INs in Disc1 mice form fewer release sites on targets.
source: The number of FS-INs is reduced, they receive fewer excitatory inputs, and form fewer release sites on targets.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by binomial analysis of uIPSCs shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Weak excitatory input and inhibitory output of FS-INs may lead to impaired gamma oscillations.
source: Computational analysis indicates that weak excitatory input and inhibitory output of FS-INs may lead to impaired gamma oscillations.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5.

claim: A Scottish family carrying a c-terminal 1:11 translocation in the DISC1 gene downstream of exon eight results in a c-terminal truncation of DISC1.
source: The original discovery came from a Scottish family carrying a large c-terminal 1:11 translocation in the DISC1 gene downstream of exon eight, which results in a c-terminal truncation of DISC1 (St Clair et al., 1990).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citation to St Clair et al., 1990.

claim: Family members affected by the DISC1 mutation suffer from mental illness including major depression (10 cases), schizophrenia (7 cases) or bipolar disorder (1 case).
source: Family members who are affected by the mutation suffer from mental illness including major depression (10 cases), schizophrenia (7 cases) or bipolar disorder (1 case, St Clair et al., 1990).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citation to St Clair et al., 1990.

claim: No major psychiatric disease was diagnosed in any of the relatives lacking DISC1 truncation (48 cases).
source: By comparison (48 cases), no major psychiatric disease was diagnosed in any of the relatives lacking DISC1 truncation.
evidence: Stated in the introduction with implicit reference to St Clair et al., 1990.

claim: Truncation of DISC1 constitutes one of the largest known risk factors for mental illness.
source: Thus, truncation of DISC1 constitutes one of the largest known risk factors for mental illness.
evidence: Stated in the introduction based on the Scottish family data.

claim: A mouse model has been developed which reproduces the human form of DISC1 truncation.
source: Recently, a mouse model has been developed which reproduces the human form of DISC1 truncation (Shen et al., 2008).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citation to Shen et al., 2008.

claim: Disc1 mice show increased immobility during the tail-suspension test (TST).
source: We find that Disc1 mice show increased immobility during the tail-suspension (TST) and forced swim test broadly accepted as depression-related behavioural changes in rodents (Porsolt et al., 1977; Steru et al., 1985).
evidence: Stated in the introduction and supported by behavioral data in Figure 1B.

claim: Disc1 mice show increased immobility during the forced swim test.
source: We find that Disc1 mice show increased immobility during the tail-suspension (TST) and forced swim test broadly accepted as depression-related behavioural changes in rodents (Porsolt et al., 1977; Steru et al., 1985).
evidence: Stated in the introduction and supported by behavioral data in Figure 1C.

claim: Increased immobility in TST and forced swim test are broadly accepted as depression-related behavioural changes in rodents.

evidence: Stated in the introduction with citations to Porsolt et al., 1977 and Steru et al., 1985.

claim: Behavioural phenotype of Disc1 mice correlates with abnormalities in the synchrony of low-gamma oscillations (30–50 Hz) in the prelimbic cortex (PrlC).
source: This behavioural phenotype correlates with abnormalities in the synchrony of low-gamma oscillations (30–50 Hz) in the prelimbic cortex (PrlC), which have been implicated in supporting encoding of information (Fries et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated in the introduction and supported by correlation analysis in Figure 2G.

claim: Low-gamma oscillations have been implicated in supporting encoding of information.

claim: Network malfunction in Disc1 mice is related to a profound defect of FS-INs, including reduced numbers of FS-INs as well as alterations in their synaptic connections.

claim: In the TST, Disc1 mice showed longer periods of immobility.

claim: In the forced swim test, Disc1 mice showed longer periods of immobility.

claim: Mean immobility in Disc1 mice was enhanced by 18% in the forced swim test (p = 0.049).

claim: Both Disc1 and control genotypes reached similar movement speeds in the open field arena.

claim: TST increased the number of cFos-positive cells in the PrlC compared to baseline in the home cage in both Disc1 and control mice.
source: By using antibody labelling against the immediate early gene cFos as a marker of neurons which underwent enhanced activity, we found that TST increased the number of cFos-positive cells in the PrlC compared to baseline in the home cage in both Disc1 and control mice, indicating that the PrlC is involved in controlling behavioural despair (Figure 2A).

claim: Prefrontal theta oscillations are driven by the hippocampus.
source: We next examined the mechanisms underlying oscillatory impairments in Disc1 PrlC. Prefrontal theta oscillations are driven by the hippocampus (Siapas et al., 2005; Sigurdsson et al., 2010) whereas gamma activity patterns are generated by synaptic interactions between GABAergic FS-INs and glutamatergic PCs in local neuronal networks (Atallah and Scanziani, 2009; Tiesinga and Sejnowski, 2009).
evidence: Stated in the results with citations to Siapas et al., 2005 and Sigurdsson et al., 2010.

claim: Gamma activity patterns are generated by synaptic interactions between GABAergic FS-INs and glutamatergic PCs in local neuronal networks.
source: We next examined the mechanisms underlying oscillatory impairments in Disc1 PrlC. Prefrontal theta oscillations are driven by the hippocampus (Siapas et al., 2005; Sigurdsson et al., 2010) whereas gamma activity patterns are generated by synaptic interactions between GABAergic FS-INs and glutamatergic PCs in local neuronal networks (Atallah and Scanziani, 2009; Tiesinga and Sejnowski, 2009).

claim: Coherence in the theta band was comparable between genotypes.

claim: Theta power was markedly reduced in CA1 of Disc1 mice.
